Turn notes into a website

16 November 2026 · Reading time: 6 minutes · Audio in the app: 8 minutes. Listening to the briefing is part of Sapaude Premium.

Google’s Gemini Notebook, formerly NotebookLM, can now turn the sources in a notebook into an interactive site you open in a new tab and share.

Sapaude retells the story in its own words. The source is below. Publisher: Sapaude.

In three points

Three points, in this order: what the source shows, where that claim stops, and what to check next.

  1. On 16 November 2026 Google said typing “make me a site” in a Gemini Notebook chat, plus a description, builds an interactive site from that notebook’s sources. The examples are an interactive periodic table, a historical timeline, a quarterly sales dashboard, and a tracker of tasks and deadlines.
  2. Google’s help pages say the generated pages can be wrong, and that a shared report link assumes the other person can open the full notebook. The site is only as solid as the sources it is built from.
  3. The web rollout started that day for Gemini Notebook users who are 18 or older, including Workspace subscribers. Google still lists the mobile app as coming soon.

A notebook that only knows your sources

Gemini Notebook is where you put the files for one piece of work and ask questions against those files. Google renamed NotebookLM to Gemini Notebook on 16 July 2026. Josh Woodward, who leads Google Labs, wrote that it is the same standalone product, a research tool, and that more than 30 million people and over 600,000 organizations were using it. Those figures are from that July post, not a new count. You add PDFs, websites, YouTube videos, audio, Google Docs, or Google Slides. The chat answers from those sources and shows citations you can open.

On 16 November 2026 Maria Ines Aranguren, a software engineer in Google Labs, wrote that the notebook can turn those sources into interactive sites, so a pile of material becomes something you click through. Google’s reason is speed on complex information, for work or for study. The line you type, the pages Google names, and the checks before you share one are the rest of it.

You describe the site in the chat

The instruction in the blog is literal. In the Gemini Notebook chat you type “make me a site” and a description of the page you want. Google’s examples are specific. For preparing for an exam, a visual explainer such as an interactive periodic table or a historical timeline. For numbers, an interactive dashboard, and the case it names is quarterly sales performance. For a project, a tracker that lays out tasks and deadlines.

When the site exists, you choose “Open in a new tab” to use it, or you share it. Google’s help center also documents interactive reports in the Studio panel. Open a notebook you can edit, choose Reports, then Interactive, and start from a Learning Overview template. Generation can take a while, and some of that content is only for people 18 and older. The blog of 16 November 2026 points at the chat line. The help article points at Studio. Google does not say the two paths produce different pages.

The chat stays with the sources. Google’s chat help says answers use quotes, text, and images from your sources as citations, and that a response is not supposed to leave those sources. With many sources, Gemini Notebook first pulls the passages that match the question and then builds the answer. The blog’s claim for the new page is the same. The site comes from the sources already in the notebook.

Wrong pages travel with the link

Google’s help page on reports says the output is generated and may contain inaccuracies or mistakes, and it tells you to review it. The general notebook help says Gemini Notebook can make mistakes and that its answers are not Google’s views. A site built from a notebook follows the sources. If a file is out of date or a table is incomplete, the announcement does not say the site will repair that. The check is against the file, not against how finished the page looks.

Sharing reaches further than a picture of the page. The blog says you can share the site. The help article for interactive reports says a report link requires the notebook to be shared already, or open to anyone with the link, and that those people have access to the full notebook. A separate help page says sharing the notebook gives a viewer the sources and the notes. A shared site hands over the material it was built from, not a cropped view of the page. Google’s notebook help also says uploads are not used to train Gemini Notebook unless you send feedback. That line is about training, not about who can open a link.

Access fits in one sentence. Google says the feature is rolling out globally on the web from 16 November 2026 for Gemini Notebook users who are 18 or older, including Google Workspace subscribers, and that the mobile app is coming soon. The help page says interactive reports are available on the web.

Build one page and check it against the file

Use a notebook you already trust, at notebook.google.com. Type “make me a site” and describe one page in the shape of Google’s examples. A timeline of the dates in your sources, one quarter’s figures, or a list of tasks and deadlines you can count by hand. Then choose “Open in a new tab”.

Before you send it to anyone, read three claims back against the original source. Take a date, a number, and one label. Google’s citations in the chat are for the written answers. The report help does not say the generated page carries those citations, so the comparison is on you. If something is off, that warning is the reason to stop.

If you do share, assume the other person can reach the notebook, because that is the condition the report help states for a report link. Skip the share when the sources include anything that person should not have. The mobile app is not the place to try this yet. Google still lists it as coming soon.

What you can do

In a notebook you already keep at notebook.google.com, type make me a site and describe one page you actually need, because the chat can now build it from those sources. Open the result in a new tab and check a few figures or dates against the original files before you rely on it. Share the link only if the other person should also reach the notebook, since Google’s help page for these reports says that access comes with the share.

In the app, the same story is also told shorter and in more detail, matched to your level.

Source: Google. Published: 16 November 2026.
